metadata.title: Project Progress: Reusable Components and Merge Strategy
metadata.purpose: Fellow-style project progress video for future developers
metadata.format_note: Canonical source beat sheet. Final deliverables render in both native 4K aspects.

beats.narration_text: Hi I am Rushali and the video is about reusable components and the merge strategy I used for the Humanitarians AI website. This update shows how the changes were made easier to maintain and safer to integrate. I will connect the page work to the branch history so the next developer can follow both the code and the delivery process.

props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI REUSABLE COMPONENTS AND MERGE STRATEGY
props.command: Show the maintainability and integration path.
props.runningText: reuse, integrate, review, and hand off...

beats.narration_text: This week I added content to the Medhavy page and looked for repeated patterns across the projects pages. The goal was not only to make one page look correct, but to leave the code easier for the next developer to extend. I treated the page as part of a larger system, checking where content belongs and which UI patterns are shared instead of adding another one-off block.

props.title: One shared component keeps pages consistent
props.subtitle: The Medhavy content work also exposed repeated project-page structure.
props.sparkLine: Change the pattern once, improve every page.

beats.narration_text: The Get Started section at the end of the projects page was inconsistent. I created a reusable ProjectGetStarted component, then used the same component wherever that section appears. This keeps markup and styling in one place instead of duplicating it across pages. A future change to the call to action, spacing, or visual treatment can therefore be made in the component and reviewed once, rather than copied manually into every project page.

props.title: Build the pattern once
props.subtitle: A shared ProjectGetStarted block makes the ending of each project page consistent.
props.sparkLine: One source of truth means fewer drift bugs.

beats.narration_text: I kept each change in its own branch while working, then planned a local integration branch for combining the completed fixes. This preserves the story of each change and gives the team one place to review the combined result before main is touched. The branch is a checkpoint: it lets me combine the work, run the application locally, and see whether individually correct changes still work correctly together.

props.title: Bring finished branches together locally
props.subtitle: The integration branch becomes a reviewable checkpoint before main.
props.code:
git switch -c integration
git merge --no-ff fix/route
git merge --no-ff fix/components

beats.narration_text: I used no-fast-forward merges so each completed branch remains visible in the history. That makes it easier to understand which fix introduced a change, review the work independently, and revert a focused change if necessary. The graph also gives reviewers context, because each merge points back to a focused piece of work rather than one large unexplained commit.

props.title: Keep the change boundaries visible
props.subtitle: The merge graph records each completed fix instead of flattening the history.
props.code:
git merge --no-ff fix/components
git log --oneline --graph
git diff main..integration

beats.narration_text: If branches change the same lines, Git pauses with a merge conflict. I would inspect the conflict markers, choose the intended combined result, remove the markers, and then run the application checks before staging the resolution. I would also check the affected page in the browser, because a conflict can be syntactically resolved while the resulting layout or behavior is still wrong.

props.title: Resolve the disagreement, then verify
props.subtitle: A conflict is a review point, not a reason to guess.
props.sparkLine: Edit deliberately, test visibly, continue safely.
props.code:
git status
# edit the conflicted file
git add <resolved-file>
git commit -m "resolve merge"

beats.narration_text: After resolving conflicts, I would compare the integration branch with main, test the visible routes and page behavior, and inspect the final diff. Only after that review would the integration branch be pushed and prepared for the pull request into main. The final review should cover the changed files, the visible behavior, the branch history, and any assumptions that the next developer needs to know.

props.title: Make the final branch easy to trust
props.subtitle: The handoff includes behavior checks, history, and a focused diff.
props.sparkLine: A clean review is part of the implementation.

beats.narration_text: The result is a maintainable component pattern and a safer integration path for future contributors. Reuse the shared component, keep branches focused, and review the combined change before it reaches main. That process keeps the repository understandable and makes the next change easier to review.

props.title: Reuse, integrate, review
props.subtitle: Project progress from Rushali for the next Humanitarians AI developer.
